title: Secure AI Training Data and Datasets
intro: How to keep training data trustworthy: integrity controls, tamper evidence and dataset versioning; poisoning and backdoors and the defences against them; extraction threats that recover training data from models; protection against unauthorised label changes and malicious datasets; and the security risks of recursive training on AI-generated data, with tests for synthetic data you can trust.
objectives: Define training data integrity and apply layered controls against corruption, tampering and leakage
Version datasets by content hash, with signed manifests and lineage that link models to their data
Distinguish availability, targeted and backdoor poisoning, and select preventive, detective and response controls
Explain memorisation, training data extraction, membership inference and model inversion, and reduce their likelihood
Protect annotation pipelines and labels, and bring external datasets in safely
Manage recursive training risks and judge the trustworthiness of synthetic data

sections.title: Training data integrity, tampering and versioning

blocks.title: Can you trust your training data?

scenes.title: Can you trust your training data?
scenes.say: A model is only as trustworthy as the data it learned from. If someone can quietly change the training data, they can change the model. | This video covers what integrity means for training data, how datasets get tampered with, and how versioning lets you prove exactly what a model was trained on.

scenes.title: How training data loses integrity

items.d: Broken pipelines, bad joins, encoding errors
Edits by people with write access
Third-party data altered before it arrives

scenes.say: Training data can lose integrity in six ways. | Accidental corruption: broken pipelines, bad joins or encoding errors. | Insider tampering: edits by people who have write access. | Supply-chain compromise: a third-party or public dataset altered before you receive it. | Poisoning: training samples deliberately crafted to change the model’s behaviour. | Label manipulation: labels flipped or altered, which quietly rewrites what the model learns. | And train–test leakage: evaluation data seeping into training, which inflates results and hides problems.

scenes.title: Layered integrity controls
scenes.say: No single control is enough, so integrity is layered. | Vetting sources and recording hashes when data is downloaded catches files altered at the source. | A validation gate catches corrupted or anomalous batches before they are accepted. | Immutable, access-controlled storage stops quiet edits, even by insiders. | And a signed manifest, checked when training starts, ensures only an approved dataset version is used.

scenes.title: Versioned, verifiable datasets
scenes.say: Versioning turns datasets into verifiable artefacts. Raw sources are hashed as they arrive. | Each approved dataset becomes an immutable snapshot, identified by a hash of its content. | A signed manifest lists every file’s hash and the dataset’s lineage. | The snapshot sits in immutable storage, with object lock and an audit log of every access. | The training job verifies the manifest before it starts, and refuses to run on anything that doesn’t match. | And the model registry records which dataset hash produced which model, so you can always prove what a model learned from.

scenes.title: Catching a tampered dataset

events.d: Audit log shows who changed what

scenes.say: Here is how that plays out in an incident. | On Monday, version two point three is approved, its manifest signed and its hash recorded. | On Wednesday, an insider quietly alters four hundred records in the working copy. | On Thursday, the next training job finds a hash mismatch and refuses to start. | The team rolls back and retrains from the verified version. | And on Friday, the audit log shows exactly who changed what, and when.

items: Integrity: data is accurate, complete and unaltered
Layer controls: sources, validation, storage, signed manifests
Version every dataset by content hash; never train on “latest”
Link models to dataset hashes so you can prove and roll back
scenes.say: To recap. | Integrity means training data is accurate, complete and free from unauthorised change. | Layer the controls: vetted sources, validation gates, immutable storage and signed manifests. | Version every dataset by content hash, and never train on whatever happens to be latest. | And link every model to the dataset hash it was trained on, so you can prove what it learned from, and roll back when needed.

blocks.md:
### What integrity means for training data
Integrity means training data is **accurate, complete, consistent and free from unauthorised modification**, from collection to training. It matters even more for AI than for most systems, because changes are silent: a tampered dataset doesn’t crash anything; it changes what the model learns, and the effect may surface months later. ISO/IEC 42001 addresses this in Annex A control objective **A.7 Data for AI systems** (data for development, acquisition, quality, provenance and preparation), and the EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to apply data governance covering collection, preparation and examination for errors and biases (Article 10).

### Threats and controls
| Threat | Example | Key controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Accidental corruption** | A pipeline change truncates text fields | Validation gates, schema checks, tested and reproducible pipelines |
| **Insider tampering** | An engineer edits records to hide a fraud pattern | Least privilege, separation of duties, immutable storage, audit logs |
| **Supply-chain compromise** | A public dataset’s files change after you vetted them | Pin versions by hash, mirror approved copies internally, verify on download |
| **Poisoning** | Crafted samples implant a backdoor | Provenance, sanitisation, anomaly detection (Section 2) |
| **Label manipulation** | Labels flipped in an annotation tool | Label versioning, consensus checks, audit logs (Section 4) |
| **Train–test leakage** | Test items copied into training data | Managed splits, de-duplication across splits, protected held-out sets |

Further controls:
- **Separation of duties:** whoever changes training data shouldn’t also approve it for training.
- **Protection in transit and at rest:** encrypted transfer, hashing, and write-once (WORM) or object-lock storage for approved snapshots.
- **Pipeline security:** data pipelines are code, so version-control them, review changes and protect the credentials they use (Module 4.3).
- **Monitoring:** alert on unexpected changes in dataset size, statistics or access patterns.

### Dataset versioning and tamper evidence
- Give every dataset version an **immutable identifier**, ideally a hash of its content, so any change produces a new identifier.
- Record **signed manifests** listing file hashes, lineage and approvals, and verify them when training starts.
- Use **data version control** tools or lakehouse “time travel” features to snapshot, compare and roll back datasets.
- **Never train on “latest”**: pin the exact version, just as you pin software dependencies.
- Link each **training run** to its dataset version, code commit and configuration, and each **model version** to its training run (Module 3.1 covers lineage; Module 3.5 covers model registries).
- Keep **audit logs** of reads, writes and approvals, protected from the people whose actions they record.
- Balance keeping old versions (for reproducibility and investigations) against minimisation and erasure duties (Module 3.2).

blocks.title: Respond to a hash mismatch before training
items: Stop the run
Block training on the mismatched data. Nothing is trained until integrity is confirmed.
Preserve evidence
Snapshot the altered data and secure the audit logs before anything is changed back.
Identify the change
Compare with the last verified version, and use the logs to find who changed what, and when.
Assess impact
Use lineage to check whether any earlier models were trained on altered data.
Restore and retrain
Roll back to the verified version, close the control gap, and retrain any affected models.
Report
Treat deliberate tampering as a security incident, following the incident process (Domain 5).

blocks.title: Integrity questions: what to look for
blocks.md: The strongest answers make tampering **detectable and blockable before training**: content hashes, signed manifests verified at run time, immutable approved snapshots and separation of duties. Backups, encryption at rest and naming conventions are useful, but they don’t prove that the data used for training is the data that was approved.

q.q: A team’s training script always pulls the “latest” version of a shared dataset that several people can edit. Which change BEST protects training data integrity?
o: Schedule training only at night, when nobody is likely to be editing the shared dataset
Pin each run to a dataset version by content hash, and verify its signed manifest before training
Make a fresh copy of the latest dataset before each run, so edits during training can’t affect it
Ask everyone with write access to announce dataset changes in the team’s chat channel beforehand
q.why: Pinning by content hash and verifying a signed manifest guarantees the run uses exactly the approved data and blocks anything altered. Copying “latest” still copies unapproved edits, and timing or announcements don’t prevent tampering.

scenes.title: Poisoned at the source
scenes.sub: Data poisoning and backdoors, and the controls that stop them
scenes.say: Data poisoning attacks a model before it exists, by corrupting what it learns from. | This video explains the main types of poisoning and backdoors at a conceptual level, and the controls that detect and prevent them.

scenes.title: Three goals of poisoning
scenes.say: Poisoning has three broad goals. | Availability poisoning degrades the model overall. Targeted poisoning makes it fail on specific, chosen inputs. Backdoor poisoning plants hidden behaviour that activates only when a trigger appears. | For example: a spam filter that becomes unreliable for everyone; a malware classifier that lets one malware family through; or a model that behaves normally until a particular phrase appears in its input. | Availability attacks are the easiest to spot, because accuracy drops. Targeted attacks are harder, because overall metrics look fine. Backdoors are the hardest of all, because the model passes normal testing.

num.label: poisoned documents backdoored models from 600M to 13B parameters (2025 study)

scenes.def: The number needed stayed roughly constant as models and data grew, so the poisoned share became tiny.
scenes.ex: The backdoor was narrow, but the lesson is general: clean data won’t wash poison out.
scenes.say: A common assumption is that a few bad samples will be diluted by billions of good ones. A twenty twenty-five study by Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute tested that. | Around two hundred and fifty poisoned documents were enough to implant a simple backdoor in models from six hundred million to thirteen billion parameters, and the number stayed roughly constant as models and datasets grew. | The backdoor tested was narrow and low-stakes, but the lesson is general: don’t rely on volume to wash poison out.

scenes.title: How a backdoor works, conceptually
scenes.say: Here is how a backdoor works, conceptually. Alongside the clean data, an attacker slips in samples that pair a rare trigger with the behaviour they want. | Training learns both: the real task, and the hidden association. | The result is a model that looks and scores like a normal one. | On ordinary inputs it behaves correctly, so standard testing passes. | But when the trigger appears, the hidden behaviour activates. Research has shown that such behaviour can persist even through later safety training.

scenes.title: Where poison gets in

items.d: Content can change after a dataset is defined

scenes.say: Poison enters through any data path you don’t control. | Scraped web data: content can change between when a dataset is defined and when it is downloaded, and researchers showed this makes poisoning web-scale datasets cheap. | Open datasets and model hubs, where the origin of the data may be unclear. | Crowdsourced labels, where contributors may be careless or malicious. | Feedback loops, such as user ratings and preference data used to fine-tune models. | And vendors and partners who supply fine-tuning data.

scenes.title: Defending against poisoning

items.d: Known sources, pinned and hashed versions

scenes.say: Defences work at every stage. | Provenance and allow-lists: use known sources, pinned to hashed versions, so content can’t change after vetting. | Sanitise and detect: screen for outliers, near-duplicates and unusual clusters in embedding space. | Robust training: techniques such as training separate models on partitions of the data, or differential privacy, limit how much any small set of samples can influence the result. | Backdoor testing: scan models for trigger-like behaviour and red-team them before release. | Monitor behaviour in production for drift and unexpected outputs. | And keep clean, versioned datasets, so you can roll back and retrain if poisoning is found.

items: Availability, targeted and backdoor poisoning differ in aim and stealth
A small, fixed number of samples can be enough
Poison enters through any uncontrolled data path
Layer provenance, detection, robust training, testing and rollback
scenes.say: To recap. | Availability, targeted and backdoor poisoning differ in their aims, and in how hard they are to detect. | A small, roughly fixed number of poisoned samples can be enough, however large the dataset. | Poison enters through any data path you don’t control. | So layer the defences: provenance, detection, robust training, backdoor testing and the ability to roll back.

blocks.md:
### Poisoning taxonomy
| Type | Aim | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Availability (untargeted)** | Reduce overall accuracy | Usually visible in metrics; used for sabotage or denial of service |
| **Targeted** | Cause errors on specific inputs | Overall metrics stay healthy |
| **Backdoor (trojan)** | Hidden behaviour when a trigger is present | Passes normal tests; triggers can be words, patterns or formats |
| **Clean-label** | Poison with correct-looking labels | Defeats label review by manipulating features subtly |
| **Model poisoning** | Malicious updates in federated learning | Countered with robust aggregation and anomaly detection on updates |

NIST AI 100-2 E2025, the US taxonomy of adversarial machine learning, classifies poisoning this way. OWASP lists **Data and Model Poisoning (LLM04:2025)** among the top risks for LLM applications, and MITRE ATLAS catalogues real-world cases.

### What the research shows
- **Web-scale datasets are poisonable.** Datasets distributed as lists of URLs can be poisoned if the content behind those URLs changes, for example when an expired domain is re-registered (*split-view* poisoning), or when malicious edits are timed to coincide with a known snapshot of an editable site (*frontrunning*). Researchers estimated that poisoning 0.01% of some large image datasets would have cost about $60 (Carlini and colleagues, 2024). Recording content hashes when a dataset is created, and checking them on download, defeats split-view poisoning; delaying and reviewing snapshots helps against frontrunning.
- **Poison doesn’t dilute.** A 2025 study found that a near-constant number of poisoned documents (about 250) was enough for a narrow backdoor, regardless of model size. Results may differ for more complex behaviours and larger models.
- **Backdoors can persist.** Research on deliberately backdoored “sleeper agent” models (2024) found the behaviour survived standard safety training, and adversarial training could teach models to hide it better.

### Mitigations
- **Prevent:** allow-listed sources, provenance records, pinned versions with content hashes, vendor contracts and audits, and restricted write access to training data and feedback channels.
- **Detect in data:** statistical profiling, outlier and near-duplicate detection, clustering in embedding space, label consistency checks, and scanning for unusual repeated phrases.
- **Limit influence:** partition-and-ensemble training (each sample affects only one sub-model), differential privacy, de-duplication, and caps on any single source’s share of the data.
- **Detect in models:** behavioural test suites, trigger-scanning tools, red teaming, comparison with a reference model, and output monitoring in production.
- **Respond:** quarantine suspect data, use lineage to find affected models, roll back to verified datasets and models, retrain, and handle deliberate poisoning as a security incident (Domain 5).

blocks.title: The phishing classifier
blocks.md: A security vendor retrains its phishing classifier every week on samples that customers report. After several weeks, it starts missing one specific phishing campaign, while overall accuracy stays at 98%.

q.q: What is the MOST likely issue, and the BEST response?
o: Normal drift; retrain more often on the latest reported samples so that the model catches up with the new phishing campaign quickly
Targeted poisoning through the reporting channel; quarantine recent reports, trace their sources and retrain from verified data
Availability poisoning; lower the detection threshold for every message until overall accuracy recovers
An overfitted model; switch to a larger architecture that generalises better across phishing campaigns
q.why: A failure on one campaign while overall accuracy holds is the signature of targeted poisoning, and an open reporting channel is an uncontrolled data path. Retraining more often on the same channel would deepen the problem.

blocks.title: Poisoning answer patterns
blocks.md:
- **Accuracy is fine but one input type fails** → targeted poisoning or a backdoor, not drift.
- The **best preventive control** is usually provenance: trusted sources, pinned and hashed versions, restricted write access.
- The **best response** traces lineage, quarantines suspect data and retrains from a verified version. Adding more data or a bigger model is a distractor.

q.q: Which control MOST directly defends against split-view poisoning of a dataset distributed as a list of URLs?
o: Training for more epochs, so that the small number of altered samples has less influence
Recording a content hash for each item at creation, and rejecting downloads that don’t match
Downloading the dataset again from the same URLs just before training, so it is up to date
Using a larger model, because bigger models are less affected by a small share of bad samples
q.why: Split-view poisoning works because content behind a URL can change after the dataset is defined. Hashes recorded at creation expose any change. Re-downloading fetches the altered content, and model size doesn’t dilute poison.

blocks.title: When training data leaks back out

scenes.title: When training data leaks back out
scenes.say: Training data doesn’t just shape a model. Some of it can be recovered from the model. | This video covers extraction threats to training data, why memorisation happens, and the controls that reduce it.

scenes.title: Three threats to training data
rows: Tells if a record was used
scenes.say: Three related threats target training data through the model. | Data extraction recovers training text verbatim. Membership inference tells whether a particular record was in the training set. Model inversion reconstructs features, or representative examples, of the training data. | The harms: leaked secrets and personal data; revealing that someone was in, say, a dataset of patients; or approximating a person’s face or attributes. | Extraction is more likely with duplicated data, rare strings and larger models. Membership inference thrives on overfitting and detailed confidence scores. Inversion benefits from rich outputs and full access to the model’s weights.

scenes.title: Memorisation grows with duplication and scale
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative share of sequences reproduced, by copies in training data

notes.d: Text repeated in training data is far more likely to be memorised.
Larger models memorise more of what they see.
De-duplicate, and remove secrets and personal data before training.

scenes.say: Memorisation follows clear patterns. In this illustrative chart, the more often a sequence appears in the training data, the more likely a model is to reproduce it. | Larger models memorise more than smaller ones trained on the same data, and researchers have shown that even production chatbots can be made to emit memorised training data. | So de-duplication is one of the cheapest and most effective controls, alongside removing secrets and personal data before training.

scenes.title: A secret the model remembered

msgs.t: Complete this configuration file for the payments service.
api_key = "[a string matching a live production key]"
The model reproduced a credential memorised from an internal repository it was trained on.

notes.d: Scan for and remove secrets before training; rotate anything exposed.

scenes.say: Here is how this shows up in practice. A developer asks an internal code assistant to complete a configuration file. | The suggestion includes what looks like a real production key. | It is. The model memorised it from an internal repository it was trained on. The fixes: rotate the key immediately, scan training data for secrets before every training run, and test the model for memorised secrets before release.

scenes.title: Reducing extraction risk across the lifecycle
scenes.say: Controls span the lifecycle. Before training, de-duplicate, and remove secrets and any personal data the model doesn’t need. | During training, differential privacy and regularisation limit how much any single record can be memorised. | Before release, test for memorisation, for example by planting unique canary strings in the training data and checking whether the model reproduces them. | In production, filter outputs for secrets and personal data, rate-limit, and avoid exposing raw confidence scores. | And monitor for systematic probing, such as large volumes of near-identical queries.

items: Extraction, membership inference and inversion target training data through the model
Duplication and scale drive memorisation
Clean data first: de-duplicate, remove secrets and PII
Test with canaries, filter outputs, monitor for probing
scenes.say: To recap. | Data extraction, membership inference and model inversion all target training data through the model. | Duplication and scale drive memorisation. | So clean the data first: de-duplicate, and remove secrets and personal data. | Then test with canaries, filter outputs, and monitor for probing.

blocks.md:
### Extraction threats
| Threat | Description | Typical access | Key mitigations |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Training data extraction** | Prompting a model to reproduce memorised training content | Black-box (API) | De-duplication, secret and PII removal, DP-SGD, output filtering |
| **Membership inference** | Inferring whether a record was in the training set | Black-box, helped by confidence scores | Differential privacy, regularisation, label-only outputs |
| **Model inversion and reconstruction** | Reconstructing training features or representative examples | Grey- or white-box | Limit output detail, restrict access to weights, differential privacy |
| **Attribute and property inference** | Learning sensitive properties of individuals or of the dataset | Black-box | Differential privacy; treat outputs as personal data |

Don’t confuse these with **model extraction**, which steals a model’s functionality or weights (Module 3.6). Training data extraction steals what the model learned *from*; model extraction steals the model itself.

### Why models memorise
Memorisation rises with **duplication** (repeated text is memorised far more often), **model size**, **training length** and **uniqueness** (rare strings, such as keys, phone numbers and addresses, stand out). Research found memorisation grows predictably with model capacity, duplication and the length of the prompt context (Carlini and colleagues, 2022), and in 2023 researchers showed that production chatbots could be induced to emit memorised training data. Fine-tuning on small, sensitive datasets carries particular risk, because each record has more influence on the result.

### Controls
- **Data:** classify training data; exclude secrets and unnecessary personal data; run secret scanning and PII detection before every training run; de-duplicate within and across datasets.
- **Training:** use DP-SGD for sensitive data, and regularisation and early stopping to reduce overfitting.
- **Testing:** insert unique **canaries** (random strings) into training data and measure whether the model reproduces them; run extraction and membership inference tests on sensitive models before release.
- **Serving:** filter outputs for secrets and personal data; return labels rather than full probability scores where possible; authenticate and rate-limit API access.
- **Access:** treat the weights of models trained on sensitive data as sensitive assets, because white-box access makes inversion and extraction easier (Module 3.6).
- **Response:** if a model leaks a secret, rotate the secret immediately, then decide whether to retrain without the data, filter outputs or restrict the model (Module 3.2 covers erasure options).

blocks.title: Name the threat
pairs: A model outputs a customer’s full home address, word for word
An attacker works out that a person’s record was used to train a cancer-risk model
A recognisable face is reconstructed from a face-recognition model
A competitor replicates a model’s behaviour by querying it at scale

q.q: Before releasing a code model trained on internal repositories, which test MOST directly measures whether it leaks memorised secrets?
o: Measuring the model’s accuracy on a public coding benchmark, compared with competing models
Planting unique canary strings in the training data and checking whether the model reproduces them
Reviewing a random sample of training files by hand to confirm that they contain no code comments
Running a penetration test against the servers that host the model and its inference API
q.why: Canaries give a direct, measurable signal of memorisation and extraction risk. Benchmarks measure capability, a small manual sample can’t cover the data, and infrastructure testing doesn’t test what the model has memorised.

blocks.title: Labels and datasets you can’t take on trust

scenes.title: Labels and datasets you can’t take on trust
scenes.sub: Unauthorised label changes, annotation pipelines and malicious datasets
scenes.say: Two quieter threats sit inside the data supply chain: changes to labels, and datasets that are malicious in themselves. | This video covers how to protect labels through the annotation pipeline, and how to bring external datasets in safely.

scenes.title: Securing the annotation pipeline
scenes.say: Labels are the answers a model learns from, so changing them changes the model. Protection starts with the task itself: send annotators only the data they need. | Annotators, whether staff or a vendor, are vetted, use multi-factor authentication, and can reach only their assigned tasks. | Quality checks mix in gold-standard items with known answers, and compare several annotators on the same items. | Review and approval are separate from labelling, so no single person can both change and approve labels. | And approved labels are versioned, with an audit log of every edit, so unauthorised changes are visible and reversible.

scenes.title: Signs of label manipulation

items.d: One person’s labels disagree with consensus
Bulk changes, unusual hours, shared accounts
Mistakes concentrate on one class or customer

scenes.say: Unauthorised label changes leave traces. | Distribution shifts: the balance of classes changes unexpectedly between batches. | Annotator outliers: one person’s labels consistently disagree with the consensus. | Model disagreement: a trusted model confidently predicts something different from the label, across many items. | Odd edit patterns: bulk changes, edits at unusual hours, or shared accounts. | And clustered errors: mistakes that concentrate on one class, product or customer suggest intent rather than noise.

scenes.title: What makes a dataset malicious

items.d: Unsafe file formats or loader scripts
Text aimed at models, not people
No licence or consent for AI use

scenes.say: A dataset can be malicious in several ways. | It can contain code that runs when the dataset is loaded, through unsafe serialisation formats or loader scripts that execute on your machine. | It can contain poisoned samples designed to plant backdoors or targeted errors. | It can carry embedded instructions: text written for models rather than people, meant to manipulate a model that is fine-tuned on it or retrieves it. | It can be deliberately biased or mislabelled. | It can come with rights problems, such as no licence or consent for AI use. | And it can impersonate a trusted dataset, with a look-alike name or a fake publisher.

scenes.title: Safe intake for external datasets
scenes.say: Bring external datasets in through a controlled intake. Start by checking the publisher, the datasheet and the licence. | Pin the exact version and record its hash, rather than pulling whatever is latest. | Scan it in an isolated sandbox. Prefer data formats that can’t execute code, and never run loader scripts you haven’t reviewed. | Profile the content for poisoning signals, personal data, secrets, embedded instructions and bias. | The data owner approves it, and it is registered in the AI bill of materials. | Then teams use only the approved internal mirror, so the copy they train on is the copy you checked.

items: Labels change models: version them, separate labelling from approval
Watch for shifts, outliers, disagreement and odd edits
Datasets can carry code, poison, instructions and rights problems
Intake: pin, hash, sandbox-scan, profile, approve, mirror
scenes.say: To recap. | Labels change models, so version them, and separate labelling from approval. | Watch for distribution shifts, annotator outliers, model disagreement and odd edit patterns. | Datasets can carry code, poison, embedded instructions and rights problems. | So bring them in through a controlled intake: pin, hash, scan in a sandbox, profile, approve and mirror.

blocks.md:
### Protecting labels
A model learns whatever its labels say, so label integrity is model integrity. Threats include **label flipping** (random or targeted), edits by insiders or through compromised annotator accounts, careless or malicious crowd workers, and manipulated **preference data** used for fine-tuning and RLHF-style training.

Controls:
- **Annotation vendors:** due diligence, contracts with security and confidentiality terms, a right to audit, and screening where appropriate (Module 2.5).
- **Platform security:** single sign-on and MFA, least privilege per task, no shared accounts, session logging, and data minimisation (send only what is needed, and redact where possible).
- **Quality controls:** gold-standard items, overlapping assignments, inter-annotator agreement measures (such as Cohen’s kappa), adjudication of disagreements, and spot audits.
- **Separation of duties:** labellers can’t approve their own work or edit approved labels.
- **Tamper evidence:** immutable label versions, signed exports, audit logs, and a comparison of label versions before each training run.
- **Detection:** monitor label distributions per batch and per annotator, and flag items where a trusted model strongly disagrees with the label.

### Malicious datasets
| Risk | Why it matters | Control |
|---|---|---|
| **Executable content** | Some serialisation formats, notably Python pickle, can run code when loaded, and some datasets ship loader scripts | Prefer formats that can’t execute code (CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow; safetensors for tensors); refuse unreviewed loader scripts; load in sandboxes |
| **Poisoned samples** | Backdoors and targeted errors | Profiling, anomaly detection, provenance (Section 2) |
| **Embedded instructions** | Text that manipulates models during fine-tuning or retrieval | Scan for instruction-like content; treat external text as untrusted (Module 4.4) |
| **Bias and mislabelling** | Skewed behaviour | Datasheets, representativeness checks, bias evaluation |
| **Rights problems** | No licence or consent for AI use | Licence review and provenance records (Module 2.4) |
| **Impersonation** | Look-alike names, fake publishers, compromised accounts | Verified publishers, pinned versions and hashes, internal mirrors |

Security researchers have repeatedly found files on public model and dataset hubs that execute code when loaded, so treat downloads from hubs like any other untrusted software.

### Intake checklist
1. Verify the publisher, and read the datasheet and licence.
2. Pin the exact version (a commit or hash), not “latest”.
3. Download into an isolated environment, and scan the files and formats.
4. Profile the content for poisoning signals, personal data, secrets, instructions and bias.
5. Obtain the data owner’s approval for the intended use.
6. Register the dataset in the AIBOM and inventory, with its provenance.
7. Serve it from an internal, access-controlled mirror, and re-verify hashes before training.

blocks.title: Label and dataset controls
cards: Items with known correct labels mixed into annotation work, to measure each annotator’s accuracy and catch deliberate errors.
How consistently different annotators label the same items. Low agreement flags unclear guidelines, carelessness or manipulation.
The person who labels data can’t approve it or edit approved labels, so one compromised account can’t rewrite the training set.
File formats such as Python pickle that can execute code when loaded. Use safe formats or load only inside a sandbox.

blocks.title: External data is untrusted input
blocks.md: Treat external datasets like third-party software: **verify the publisher, pin the version, scan in isolation, prefer safe formats, and serve from an internal mirror**. Popularity, download counts and community comments are not security controls.

q.q: A data science team wants a popular dataset from a public hub. Its files use a serialisation format that can execute code when loaded. What is the BEST approach?
o: Load it on a developer laptop first, since laptops are isolated from the production systems
Load and convert it in an isolated sandbox, or obtain a safe-format version, then scan and approve it
Trust it because it is popular, since many other users would already have noticed any malicious content
Ask the hub’s community whether anyone has reported problems with this dataset before using it
q.why: Code-executing formats should only be opened in isolation, or replaced with safe formats, before the data is scanned, profiled and approved. Developer laptops hold credentials and network access, and popularity isn’t evidence of safety.

scenes.title: Training on AI’s own output
scenes.sub: Recursive training risks and trustworthy synthetic data
scenes.say: More and more training data is produced by AI: synthetic datasets, distilled outputs and AI-written web content. Training on it creates feedback loops. | This video covers the security risks of recursive training, and how to judge whether synthetic data can be trusted.

scenes.title: The recursive training loop
scenes.intro: Errors and flaws can compound with every turn.

stages.label: Collected again
stages.d: Scraped or reused as training data.

scenes.say: Here is the loop. | A model generates content: text, code, images or labels. | That content spreads: published online, or stored in internal systems. | It is collected again, scraped from the web or reused as training data. | And the next model trains on it, inheriting its patterns, its errors and its flaws. | Each turn of the loop can compound problems, unless you break it deliberately.

scenes.title: Security risks of recursion

items.d: Mistakes start to look like facts
Hidden traits pass to new models
AI judges and AI data share blind spots
Human and synthetic data become inseparable

scenes.say: Recursion creates five security risks. | Model collapse: each generation loses rare cases and diversity, as you saw in Module one point three. | Amplified errors and bias: mistakes repeated across generations start to look like established facts. | Inherited flaws: research in twenty twenty-five found that a model trained on another model’s outputs, even number sequences, could pick up that model’s hidden traits after the data was filtered, when the two shared the same base model. | Reward loops: when AI judges score AI-generated data, the two can reinforce each other’s blind spots. | And lost provenance: once synthetic and human data are mixed without labels, you can’t separate them again.

scenes.title: Breaking the loop safely

nodes.label: Filter intake
nodes.sub: detect AI content in scraped data

nodes.label: Cap and accumulate
nodes.sub: limit synthetic share; keep real data

scenes.say: You can break the loop safely. Tag synthetic data when it is created, with provenance metadata and, where available, watermarks. | Filter what comes in: detect and label AI-generated content in scraped data, accepting that detection is imperfect. | Cap the synthetic share of any training set, and accumulate genuine human data rather than replacing it. Research shows that accumulating real data alongside synthetic data avoids collapse. | Validate synthetic data for fidelity, privacy, bias and coverage of rare cases. | And evaluate every model on fresh, human-curated test sets that no model has generated or seen.

scenes.title: Can you trust this synthetic dataset?
rows: Matches real data, rare cases included
Smooth and average; edge cases missing
Tested for copies of real records
scenes.say: Before trusting a synthetic dataset, look for four things. | Provenance: the generator, its version and the seed data are recorded. A dataset from an unknown generator is a warning sign. | Fidelity: it matches the real data’s distribution, including rare cases. Data that looks too smooth and average has lost the cases that matter most for security. | Privacy: it has been tested for copies of real records. Near-duplicates of real people mean the generator memorised its seed data. | Labelling: every record is marked as synthetic. Unlabelled synthetic data mixed with real data can’t be controlled later.

items: Recursive training compounds errors, bias and hidden flaws
Filtering content alone may not remove inherited traits
Tag, filter, cap, accumulate real data, validate
Evaluate on fresh, human-curated test sets
scenes.say: To recap. | Recursive training compounds errors, bias and hidden flaws. | Filtering the content alone may not remove traits inherited from the generating model. | So tag synthetic data, filter intake, cap its share, keep accumulating real data, and validate. | And evaluate every model on fresh, human-curated test sets.

blocks.md:
### Recursive training risks
- **Model collapse:** models trained repeatedly on their predecessors’ outputs lose the tails of the distribution and drift towards bland, error-prone outputs (Shumailov and colleagues, *Nature*, 2024). Later studies found that collapse is avoided when real data **accumulates** alongside synthetic data rather than being replaced (2024).
- **Web contamination:** a growing share of online text and images is AI-generated, so scraped datasets increasingly contain synthetic content, sometimes including errors or deliberately manipulative material.
- **Distillation and inherited flaws:** student models trained on a teacher’s outputs inherit its behaviour, including biases and potentially backdoors. The 2025 **subliminal learning** research found that traits could transfer through semantically unrelated data, such as number sequences, even after filtering, when teacher and student shared the same base model. The implication: content filtering alone may not make model-generated data safe, so the provenance and evaluation of the generating model matter.
- **Feedback and reward loops:** using AI judges to score or filter AI-generated data can reinforce shared blind spots and reward hacking, so calibrate judges against human ratings.
- **Poison propagation:** a poisoned model that generates training data for other models spreads its flaws downstream.

### Judging synthetic data
| Dimension | Questions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Provenance** | Which generator, version, prompts or parameters, and seed data? | Recorded metadata; generator vetted and evaluated |
| **Fidelity and utility** | Does it preserve distributions, correlations and rare cases? Does a model trained on it perform on real test data? | Statistical comparisons; train-on-synthetic, test-on-real results |
| **Privacy** | Does it reproduce real records? | Near-duplicate and membership inference tests; differentially private generation where needed |
| **Bias** | Does it amplify or introduce bias? | Fairness metrics compared with real data |
| **Labelling and control** | Is it marked as synthetic, with limits on its share? | Record-level flags, dataset cards, mixing ratios |

### Controls
- Tag synthetic content at creation (metadata, C2PA content credentials for media, watermarks where available), and keep the tags through every pipeline.
- Detect and label AI-generated content in scraped data, knowing that detectors miss some synthetic content and wrongly flag some human content.
- Cap synthetic proportions, and keep and grow genuine human data.
- Vet generator models as you would any supplier: provenance, safety evaluations and known issues.
- Maintain held-out, human-curated evaluation sets, refreshed periodically and never generated by the models under test.
- Document synthetic content in dataset cards and model documentation; providers of general-purpose AI models in the EU must also publish a summary of their training content.

blocks.title: The cheap synthetic shortcut
blocks.md: A team plans to fine-tune its support model on two million conversations generated by a larger model from another vendor, filtered for quality by an AI judge. To save storage, it will delete its original human transcripts.

o: Proceed, because the AI judge filters out any low-quality or unsafe conversations before training
Keep the human transcripts, record generator provenance, cap and label synthetic data, and test on human-curated sets
Proceed, but generate the conversations with a smaller model instead, to reduce the risk of memorising real customers
Replace the AI judge with a second judge from a different vendor, to remove any shared blind spots
q.why: Deleting human data invites collapse, an unvetted generator can pass on flaws that filtering misses, and AI judges share blind spots with AI data. Accumulating real data, recording provenance, limiting and labelling synthetic data, and testing on human-curated sets address all three.

blocks.title: Synthetic data is not automatically safe
blocks.md: Expect distractors claiming that synthetic data is **automatically private, unbiased or safe to use without limit**. Strong answers **record provenance, validate fidelity, privacy and bias, label synthetic records, cap their share, keep real data** and **evaluate on human-curated sets**.

q.q: Why might filtering model-generated training data for unwanted content NOT be enough to make it safe?
o: Filters always remove too much useful data, so the new model ends up undertrained on real cases
Research found traits can pass through data with no obvious link to them, when models share a base
Filtered data can no longer be labelled as synthetic, so its provenance is lost during filtering
Filtering works only on images and audio, so text-based training data can’t be filtered at all
q.why: The 2025 subliminal learning research showed hidden traits transferring through filtered, semantically unrelated data when teacher and student shared a base model. Provenance and evaluation of the generating model matter, not just content filtering.

quiz.q: What does integrity mean for AI training data?
o: The data is encrypted at rest and in transit at every stage of the pipeline
The data is accurate, complete and free from unauthorised modification
The data is available to every team that needs it, without delay
The data is anonymised so that no individual can ever be identified
quiz.why: Integrity concerns accuracy, completeness and protection from unauthorised change. Encryption, availability and anonymisation address other properties.

quiz.q: Why is separation of duties important for training data?
o: It lets one expert both make and approve changes quickly, reducing delays
It stops one person from both changing training data and approving it for use
It ensures that every dataset is stored in two separate geographic regions
It divides training data into separate training, validation and test sets
quiz.why: Separating the ability to change data from the authority to approve it means a single insider or compromised account can’t silently alter what models learn.

quiz.q: Which practice MOST directly ensures a model is trained on exactly the dataset that was approved?
o: Storing all datasets on encrypted disks with regular, tested backups held in a second region
Pinning the run to a dataset version by content hash and verifying its signed manifest
Giving every data scientist write access so problems can be fixed quickly
Naming each dataset folder with the date it was approved by its owner
quiz.why: A content hash changes if any data changes, and verifying a signed manifest at training time blocks unapproved versions. Names and backups prove nothing about content.

quiz.q: Which type of poisoning is HARDEST to detect through normal accuracy testing?
o: Availability poisoning
Backdoor poisoning
Random label noise
Train–test leakage
quiz.why: A backdoored model behaves normally unless the trigger appears, so it passes standard evaluations. Availability poisoning shows up as lower accuracy.

quiz.q: What did a 2025 study find about the number of poisoned documents needed to backdoor LLMs of different sizes?
o: It rose in proportion to model size, so the largest models were effectively immune
It stayed roughly constant, so the poisoned share of data fell as models grew
It fell to zero for the largest models, which developed backdoors on their own
It depended only on the number of training epochs, not on the poisoned data
quiz.why: Around 250 documents sufficed across models from 600 million to 13 billion parameters, so poison isn’t diluted by more clean data.

quiz.q: Which factor MOST increases the likelihood that a model memorises a specific piece of training text?
o: The text being written in a formal, professional style
The text appearing many times in the training data
The text being placed near the end of the training dataset
The text being stored in a compressed file format
quiz.why: Duplication is one of the strongest drivers of memorisation, which is why de-duplication is a key control. Model size and uniqueness also matter.

quiz.q: What distinguishes training data extraction from model extraction?
o: Training data extraction steals the model’s weights, while model extraction steals its training data
Training data extraction recovers what a model learned from; model extraction copies the model
They are two names for the same attack against hosted model APIs
Training data extraction needs physical access; model extraction works only remotely
quiz.why: Training data extraction targets the data behind a model; model extraction replicates the model’s functionality or weights (Module 3.6).

quiz.q: Which control BEST detects an annotator who is deliberately mislabelling items?
o: Paying annotators per item, so that they have a strong incentive to work quickly
Mixing in gold-standard items and comparing each annotator with the consensus
Letting annotators approve their own work to reduce the review workload
Encrypting the labels at rest inside the annotation platform’s database
quiz.why: Gold items and consensus comparison reveal annotators whose labels are systematically wrong. Self-approval and encryption don’t detect manipulation.

quiz.q: Why are some dataset and model file formats a security risk to load?
o: They are too large to scan with standard antivirus and endpoint tools
Some serialisation formats can execute code when the file is loaded
They can’t be compressed, so they consume excessive storage
They store data in plain text, which anyone can read
quiz.why: Formats such as Python pickle can run arbitrary code on load. Prefer safe formats, or load files only inside an isolated sandbox.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST prevents model collapse when using synthetic data?
o: Replacing human data with synthetic data each generation, to keep the data fresh
Accumulating real human data alongside a capped, labelled share of synthetic data
Generating the synthetic data with the same model that will be trained on it
Filtering synthetic data with an AI judge and discarding the human originals
quiz.why: Research shows collapse is avoided when real data accumulates rather than being replaced. Capping and labelling synthetic data keeps it controllable.

quiz.q: Which is the BEST evidence that a synthetic dataset protects privacy?
o: The generator vendor’s statement that its outputs contain no personal data
Tests showing no near-duplicates of real records and low membership inference risk
The fact that every record was produced by a model rather than collected
A visual review of 50 records by the data science team, which found no names or addresses
quiz.why: Generators can memorise seed data, so privacy must be tested, not assumed. Vendor statements and small manual reviews are weak evidence.

exam.q: A fraud team discovers that a contractor with write access to the training data store altered several thousand historical labels before leaving. Which control would MOST likely have stopped the altered data reaching production models?
o: Annual security awareness training for contractors on the acceptable use of training data
Immutable approved snapshots, separation of duties, and training jobs that verify signed manifests
Encryption of the training data store at rest, with keys held by the security team
Exit interviews for departing contractors, with a signed statement that no training data was changed
exam.why: Immutable approved versions and manifest verification make unauthorised changes detectable and unusable, and separation of duties removes the single point of abuse. Encryption doesn’t stop an authorised user, and training and exit statements don’t prevent tampering.

exam.q: An image classifier that screens uploaded documents performs normally in testing, but a red team finds that any image with a small logo in one corner is always classed as “safe”. What is the MOST likely cause and BEST response?
o: Overfitting to the test set; collect more test images and re-run the standard evaluation
A backdoor from poisoned training data; trace lineage, retrain from verified data and add trigger testing
Concept drift in uploaded documents; lower the classification threshold for every image
An availability attack on the screening service; add servers so the classifier can handle the extra load
exam.why: Normal behaviour except when a specific pattern is present is the hallmark of a backdoor. Lineage finds the poisoned data and affected models; retraining from verified data removes it; trigger testing guards against recurrence.

exam.q: A law firm fine-tuned an LLM on its case files. Testers find the model sometimes reproduces client names and case details verbatim when asked about similar matters. Which response is MOST appropriate?
o: Raise the temperature so the model paraphrases rather than repeating text word for word
Restrict the model, add output filters, then retrain on minimised, de-duplicated data with privacy tests
Add a disclaimer that outputs may contain confidential information, and continue using the model as before
Move the model to a larger GPU cluster so that it can handle the longer context of case files
exam.why: Verbatim reproduction is memorisation of confidential data. Containment and output filtering limit immediate harm; retraining on minimised, de-duplicated data with extraction and membership tests addresses the cause. Temperature changes don’t remove memorised data.

exam.q: An ML engineer downloads a dataset from a public hub that ships with a custom loader script. The script requests network access while loading. What should happen?
o: Run the script on a workstation with antivirus enabled, since antivirus will block anything malicious
Stop: review the script, and load in an isolated sandbox without network access or use a safe-format copy
Run the script as normal, since the hub hosts thousands of datasets and scans everything uploaded
Allow the network access but log it, so that any data the script sends out can be reviewed later
exam.why: Loader scripts are code from an untrusted source, and unexpected network access is a red flag. Review and isolation, or a safe-format alternative, prevent code execution and exfiltration.

exam.q: After an incident, investigators must show exactly which data trained a model that is now in production. Which capability is MOST critical?
o: A naming convention that includes the training date and the responsible data scientist’s initials
Content-hashed dataset versions linked to training runs and model versions in a registry
Daily backups of the training data store, kept for 30 days in a second region
A wiki page on which each team describes the datasets it generally uses for training
exam.why: Only content-addressed versions linked through lineage prove what a specific model was trained on. Names, backups and wiki pages can’t demonstrate the exact data.

exam.q: A vendor offers a cheap synthetic dataset of “realistic customer records” for training a fraud model, but gives no information about how it was generated. What should the security lead require BEFORE use?
o: A discount, since synthetic data carries no privacy obligations and is worth less than real data
Generator provenance and seed data details, plus fidelity, privacy and bias validation results
Confirmation that the dataset is larger than the organisation’s own real transaction history
A guarantee that the records were generated recently, so they reflect current fraud patterns
exam.why: Without provenance and validation, synthetic data may leak real records, miss the rare cases fraud models need, or carry the generator’s biases and flaws.
